design_detail: National passive surveillance report (CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, 24 January 2020, with state and local health departments and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists) on e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) as of 14 January 2020. States and jurisdictions voluntarily reported confirmed and probable hospitalized or deceased patients to CDC each week using CDC case definitions and a national case report form (linked documents, not read). The report describes 2,668 hospitalized patients (age, sex, race and ethnicity, case status), the substances they reported using in vaping products in the 3 months before symptom onset (limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance), weekly hospital admissions, and trends in possible EVALI-related emergency department visits from the National Syndromic Surveillance Program (a query on vaping products in the stated reason for the visit; about 70% of emergency visits nationwide). No product or patient samples are tested in this report, and there is no comparison group.
can_establish: How many people had been reported to CDC as hospitalized with this lung injury by 14 January 2020, who they were, what they said they had vaped, and when weekly admissions and related emergency visits rose and fell between August 2019 and January 2020.
cannot_establish: What caused the injury (nothing was tested in this report; it relies on other work for vitamin E acetate); how many people were affected out of all who vape, or out of all who vape cannabis (no denominator); how severe the illnesses were or how many people died (not reported here); whether what patients said they vaped was what was in the device; whether every reported case was EVALI (the authors say the case definition favored sensitivity over specificity); and the full size of the outbreak (voluntary reporting; product information missing for a quarter of patients).

sample.recruitment: Not a sample: all cases reported by the 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico as of 14 January 2020, by voluntary weekly reporting using CDC case definitions (main text, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Confirmed and probable hospitalized or deceased EVALI patients meeting the CDC surveillance case definition (not reproduced in the report). Substance-use percentages are limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset (Table footnotes).
sample.demographics: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); age groups 13 to 17 years 404 (15%), 18 to 24 979 (37%), 25 to 34 631 (24%), 35 to 44 335 (13%), 45 to 64 223 (9%), 65 and over 47 (2%) of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 with sex (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 1,360 (73%) non-Hispanic white, 64 (3%) Black, 12 (1%) American Indian or Alaska Native, 38 (2%) Asian, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, 97 (5%) other, and 285 (15%) Hispanic.
sample.attrition: Product-use information was missing for 24% of patients (646 of 2,668; editors' count), and many patients were not interviewed because of loss to follow-up, refusal, or lack of resources (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Race and ethnicity were missing for about 30% (812 of 2,668; editors' count). The admissions figure shows 2,398 patients, so 270 reported patients are not in it (editors' count; the report gives no reason).
sample.selection_effects: Cases are those clinicians recognized, hospitals admitted, health departments classified and states chose to report; about half (47%) are 'probable' rather than 'confirmed'. The authors say the high sensitivity of the case definition likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). People with milder illness who were not hospitalized are outside the report.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported by patients (interview or case report form; who interviewed and how is not described) as substances used in e-cigarette, or vaping, products in the 3 months before symptom onset: any THC-containing product, any nicotine-containing product, both, exclusive THC, exclusive nicotine, neither. No laboratory confirmation of the products or of the patients' exposures in this report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported: no product type (cartridge or other), brand, source, amount, frequency or duration. The report says vaping or dabbing and that CDC advises against products from informal sources, but gives no numbers on sources.
exposure.polysubstance: Nicotine and THC product use were recorded together as categories: both 834 (41%), exclusive THC 669 (33%), exclusive nicotine 274 (14%), neither reported 44 (2%) among the 2,022 with information. Other substances, additives and contaminants cannot be captured by self-report; the authors say patients may not know the content of what they vaped.

comparison.controls: None in this report. For context, the report notes a low but long-standing background rate of emergency visits related to vaping products before the outbreak, which could reflect chemicals of concern in nicotine products or sporadic cases from the same substances that later spread (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: There is no denominator of people who vape THC or nicotine products, no comparison with people who vape and were not ill, no information on source, device, additive or amount, and no testing in this report, so the share of patients who used THC products says nothing about the risk to a person who does.

outcomes.instruments: CDC surveillance case definitions (confirmed, probable; not reproduced); weekly count of hospital admissions by week of admission (Figure 1, an image); National Syndromic Surveillance Program rate of possible EVALI-related emergency visits per million (Figure 2, an image), using a query on vaping products in the stated reason for the visit, excluding injuries such as device explosions and accidental ingestion of e-liquid but not acute THC intoxication or nicotine poisoning.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say the exposure query in the emergency data may have been affected by public and clinical awareness of the outbreak, and that coverage of the system is uneven across and within states and changes over time (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Severity beyond hospitalization (intensive care, ventilation, death) is not reported in this update; the report speaks of hospitalized or deceased patients but gives no count of deaths.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive. 2,668 hospitalized patients; among 2,022 with substance information (76% of cases), any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%), any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%), both 834 (41%), exclusive THC 669 (33%), exclusive nicotine 274 (14%), neither 44 (2%). Editors' calculation: 1,650 of all 2,668 patients (62%) is the least that reported any THC-containing product, if none of the 646 with no information had. Weekly hospital admissions peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since. Possible EVALI-related emergency visits rose by a mean of 26 per million per week (95% CI 18 to 33) between 11 August and 8 September 2019, peaked at 116 per million in the week of 8 September, fell by about 4 per million per week (95% CI 4 to 5) to 35 per million in the week of 5 January 2020, which is still above 23 per million in the week of 18 August 2019.
analysis.selective_reporting: The report is a descriptive update that cites earlier CDC updates (October and November 2019, and a January 2020 product and demographic update) for other characteristics; deaths, intensive care use and product sources are not given here.

interpretation_gap.results_show: By 14 January 2020, 2,668 people in every US state, Washington DC and two territories had been reported as hospitalized with this lung injury; they were young (median 24, three quarters under 35), two thirds male and mostly non-Hispanic white. Among the 76% with substance information, 82% said they had used a THC-containing vaping product (33% only THC products) and 57% a nicotine-containing product (14% only nicotine products). Weekly admissions and related emergency visits peaked in September 2019 and fell steadily afterwards.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report concludes that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to the outbreak (a conclusion drawn from another paper, not shown here), that the evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern in THC or non-THC products in some cases, and that the decline might be multifactorial (public awareness, removal of vitamin E acetate from products, enforcement). CDC's recommendation to avoid THC vaping products, especially from informal sources, and its advice to adults who vape instead of smoking are statements of advice, not findings of this report. Gaps: (1) the abstract's and the Summary box's percentages are of patients with information, stated as 'of EVALI patients', without the 24% with no information; (2) the exclusive categories do not add up with the 'any' categories (reporting issue 1); (3) the reasons offered for the decline are not tested, and the suggestion that vitamin E acetate was removed from products cites two news articles; (4) no number is given for deaths or for how people obtained products. The report is open about its limits and about the unexplained 14% who reported only nicotine products.

timeline.event: Earlier CDC updates in October and November 2019 (Moritz et al.; Chatham-Stephens et al.; cited in this report's reference list, not read) described patients in the same outbreak.
Laboratory analysis of lung fluid from patients, cited here for the link with vitamin E acetate
This update: 2,668 hospitalized patients and the decline in cases after September 2019.

replication.where_it_stands: A cumulative surveillance snapshot, not a study that can be replicated. Its counts are firmer than its product-use shares, which are self-reported and missing for a quarter of patients. Deaths and the later course of the outbreak are not covered by this update.

funding.funder: Not stated as a grant. Authors are staff of CDC centers (injury, immunization and respiratory diseases, chronic disease, surveillance, birth defects, minority health, environmental health, toxic substances) and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists, with a task force of state health department staff; the report is a CDC publication.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed the ICMJE disclosure form and no potential conflicts of interest were disclosed.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are the agency that ran the investigation and issued the public recommendations discussed; the report describes its own surveillance. A government health agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry.

what_would_settle_it: A case-control or cohort study of people with and without lung injury, interviewed with the devices in hand, with products tested for contents and source, with the denominator of people who vape and which products they used, and with outcomes (intensive care, ventilation, death, recovery) followed for months.

domains.note: Voluntary reporting by states; 47% of cases are 'probable'; the authors say the sensitive definition lowered specificity and may include people without EVALI. Counts of hospitalized patients are probably an undercount of all lung injury and may include some other illnesses.
Missing for 24% of patients (646 of 2,668); many were not interviewed; the 2,022 with data may differ from those without. Race and ethnicity are missing for about 30%.

Patients may not know or may not report what was in a device, and the authors say so; no sample was tested in this report; the 14% who reported only nicotine products are explained by misreporting, misclassification or true exclusive nicotine use without telling which.

domains.domain: Separation of surveillance findings from inference about cause
domains.note: The report states that its evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals and that reasons for the decline might be multifactorial, but the vitamin E acetate link and the effects of awareness, product removal and enforcement are not tested here; advice is mixed with findings.
The exclusive and any product categories do not reconcile; the abstract's shares are of patients with data; the under-35 share is 76% in the text and 76.9% from the table counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a national surveillance case series (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for surveillance counts. The report is a clear description of who was reported as hospitalized and when, by an agency with access to the case reports, and the counts of patients and their age and sex are reasonably firm descriptions of reported cases. Its product-use shares are self-reported and incomplete and cannot show what was in any product. It may be cited for the number and characteristics of hospitalized patients reported to CDC by 14 January 2020, the share who said they had used THC-containing or nicotine-containing products among those asked, and the timing of the September 2019 peak. It may not be cited for the cause of EVALI, for the risk to any person who vapes, for the proportion of patients who used illicit or informally sourced products, for deaths, or for what the decline was due to.

key_findings.finding: As of 14 January 2020, all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico had reported 2,668 hospitalized EVALI patients to CDC: 1,401 (53%) confirmed and 1,267 (47%) probable cases.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Case status row)

key_findings.finding: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); 404 (15%) aged 13 to 17, 979 (37%) 18 to 24, 631 (24%) 25 to 34, 335 (13%) 35 to 44, 223 (9%) 45 to 64, 47 (2%) 65 and over, of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 73% non-Hispanic white and 15% Hispanic. The text says 76% were under 35 (404 + 979 + 631 = 2,014 of 2,619 is 76.9%, editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Sex, Median age, Age group, Race/Ethnicity rows)

key_findings.finding: Among 2,022 patients with information on substances used (76% of 2,668): any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%); any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%); both 834 (41%); exclusive THC 669 (33%); exclusive nicotine 274 (14%); neither 44 (2%). Limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Substances used rows and footnotes)
key_findings.note: The four exclusive categories add to 1,821, not 2,022, and 1,650 minus 834 is 816, not 669 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since (Figure 1 is titled N = 2,398 patients, 270 fewer than the 2,668 reported, with no reason given; values not extracted from the image).
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title

key_findings.finding: Possible EVALI-related emergency visits (National Syndromic Surveillance Program) rose by a mean of 26 per million per week (95% CI 18 to 33) from 11 August to 8 September 2019, peaked at 116 per million in the week of 8 September, and fell by about 4 per million per week (95% CI 4 to 5) to 35 per million in the week of 5 January 2020, still above 23 per million in the week of 18 August 2019.
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 title

key_findings.finding: The authors state that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to THC-containing products used by patients (citing the lung fluid study), that a minority of patients consistently report only nicotine-containing products (possible reasons: patients may not report or know the content of what they vaped, some cases may be misclassified because the case definition was sensitive rather than specific, or the reports may be accurate), and that evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern in THC or non-THC products in some cases.
key_findings.note: The abstract and Discussion state the vitamin E acetate link; the data behind it are in the cited paper, not in this report.

key_findings.finding: Possible reasons for the decline after mid-September 2019 given by the authors (not tested): public awareness and actions by people who vape, removal of vitamin E acetate from THC products after the link was identified (supported by two news articles in footnotes), and enforcement affecting supply from informal sources. Also noted: it is not known whether additives other than vitamin E acetate could cause similar injury, and long-term consequences need long-term follow-up.

Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system is uneven and changes over time.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's mutually exclusive categories (exclusive THC 669, exclusive nicotine 274, both 834, neither 44) add to 1,821 of the 2,022 patients with information; and 'any THC' (1,650) minus 'both' (834) is 816, not 669, while 'any nicotine' (1,162) minus 'both' is 328, not 274.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 201 patients (10%) are in none of the four categories; the report does not say who they are (for example, THC use reported but nicotine unknown). The 'exclusive' shares should not be summed with 'both' to get 'any'.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 82% of EVALI patients used any THC-containing product and 57% any nicotine-containing product, but these are shares of the 2,022 with information (76%), not of the 2,668 reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: A share 'of EVALI patients' overstates what is known; the least that is known is 62% (1,650 of 2,668) for THC (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 76% of patients were under 35, while the table counts give 2,014 of 2,619 (76.9%); the 76% is the sum of the rounded table percentages (15 + 37 + 24).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Age group)
reporting_issues.consequence: A rounding artefact of 1 percentage point; no effect on interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: The suggestion that vitamin E acetate was removed from THC products and so contributed to the decline is supported by two news articles (footnotes ¶ and **), a state recall report and FDA statements; no data on product contents after the outbreak are presented.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the explanations for the decline as the authors' conjecture.

reporting_issues.issue: Race and ethnicity are available for 1,856 of 2,668 patients (70%), sex for 2,606, age for 2,619, and the figure for 2,398; percentages use these differing denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The race composition rests on 70% of cases and may differ for the rest.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7367698 (all sections, the Table, figure titles, footnotes and reference list read as text; Figures 1 and 2 are images and their values were not extracted; the linked CDC case definition and case report form were not opened)
